report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≥ .293", Text = "Follow-up comparisons likewise showed no reliable differences between the A > B and A < B groups within any individual experiment, all ps ≥ .293."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

live_data_statements: This pattern has been observed when participants are less certain about the causal status of the cue generating the smaller individual prediction error than about that of the cue generating the larger error.

These results indicated that the cue about which participants were relatively less certain underwent more changes in its associative strength, despite generating the smaller individual prediction error during the compound training. Spicer et al. therefore proposed that, when encountering an unexpected outcome, people would protect the belief about the causal status of the more certain cue and attribute the outcome to the less certain one.

Separate experiments using forced-choice confidence judgments indicated that participants were relatively more certain about the causal status of the inhibitory cue B than about the excitatory cue A. In the compound-test experiments, initial training was followed by compound training under associative-gain conditions (e.g., AB+) and a final test of outcome expectations for AD and BC.

In Experiments 1 and 3, participants rated AD lower than BC, indicating greater associative change for B, the cue with the larger individual prediction error and about which participants were expected to be relatively more certain.

In Experiment 2, however, participants rated BC lower than AD, indicating greater associative change for A, the cue generating the smaller individual prediction error and about which participants were expected to be relatively less certain.
At the final test phase (Test 2), participants provided outcome expectation ratings for the test compounds AD and BC.
Participants were asked to imagine themselves as medical doctors examining which foods influence a medical condition characterized by chronic inflammation.

text.text: Images of foods (apple, banana, broccoli, carrot, coconut, cherry, lemon, pear, orange, grape, kiwi, pineapple) were used as cues.
For each participant, fruit images were randomly assigned to cues A, W, E, C, Z, F, X, B, D, H, J, and K.

Outcomes were displayed on a bidirectional segmented color band (21 segments) ranging from green at -10 (strong decrease) to yellow at 0 (no change) to red at +10 (strong increase), with a gradual color transition between three main levels.
An arrow labeled "Decrease in
Inflammation" pointed toward -10 and an arrow labeled "Increase in Inflammation" pointed toward the +10 extreme.
The starting part of the outcome (0) was labeled "No Change."
On each trial, the outcome was indicated by an empty square positioned on the relevant segment.
Images of meals appeared at the center of the screen (height and width = 0.2).
When two foods formed a compound, they were presented side-by-side, separated by a plus sign, with left-right positions randomized on each presentation.
Participants were told that the effect of the meals on inflammation had been recorded over several months.
A progress bar at the top of the screen, accompanied by a month icon, was displayed to represent the passage of time across training and test.
Design.
Participants completed a within-subjects design (Table 1).
text.formatted: Participants completed a within-subjects design (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In Training 1, they learned three types of cue-outcome associations in which food cues were followed by a strong decrease in inflammation, no change, or by a strong increase in inflammation.
Within each block, AW, CZ, and X were always followed by a strong increase (+10), whereas EW, FZ, XB, and XD were followed by no change (0).
Food cue H was consistently followed by a strong decrease in inflammation (-10).
Training 1 comprised 80 trials divided into 10 blocks, each block containing one presentation of each of the eight trial types (AW+10, EW0, CZ+10, FZ0, X+10, XB0, XD0, H-10).
Trials were presented in random order, with the restriction that the last trial of one block and the first trial of the next block could not display the same trial type.

In Training 2, participants received 10 trials divided into five blocks, each block comprising one presentation of the critical compound AB, followed by a strong decrease (-10), and one presentation of a filler compound JK, followed by a strong increase (+10).
During each test stage, each individual or compound cue was presented once for the expectation rating, immediately followed by the confidence rating.
The testing order of the cues was randomized across participants.
Procedure.
After reading an information sheet and giving their consent, participants answered questions about demographics information.
Participants then received instructions/ cover story as follows:
Please imagine that you are a medical doctor.
A patient's medical record covering several months has been presented to you.
This patient suffers from a medical condition that results in chronic inflammation.
It has been determined that this condition is influenced by diet.
After consuming certain foods, the patient's inflammation level increases, while it decreases after consuming other foods, and some foods have no effect on inflammation at all.
Your task is to identify which foods influence the inflammation level, how strongly they do so, and which foods have no effect.
The data provided was collected over several months.
The effect of each food on the patient was recorded every time it was consumed.
Naturally, as with many things in life, the relationship between a food and its effect might change over time.

However, based on the data from several months and numerous instances of consumption for each food, you should be able to determine the relationship between each food and its impact on inflammation at the given time.
You will see the meals the patient consumed and be asked to predict their effect on the inflammation level.
After submitting your prediction, you will receive feedback about the actual outcome.
This process will repeat for each meal.
A meal may consist of either one or two foods.
At first, you may need to guess; however, over time, you will learn how the different foods influence the inflammation level, allowing you to make more accurate predictions.
To provide your prediction please use the rating scale that will be presented with the meal.
After submitting your prediction, you will be shown the actual outcome of the meal on the inflammation level on a colored segmented scale (as shown in the image below).
The outcome of each meal is indicated by one of the 21 segments
Strong Increase in Inflammation) on this scale.
Use this feedback to learn about the foods and their outcome on inflammation.
[the exemplary image of the outcome] Accuracy is more important than speed for all your answers.
Please do not take any notes during the experiment.
Press the space bar to continue the experiment.
In the training trials, either an individual or a compound cue was presented in the center of the screen.
A text displayed above the cue stated: "The meal is:" and a text below prompted participants to make their prediction based on the cue: "What outcome do you expect the meal to have on inflammation?
Please use your mouse to rate."
Participants provided their predictions using the rating scale ranging from "-10: Strong decrease in inflammation" to "0:
No change" to "+10: Strong increase in inflammation".
Clicking at any point on the rating scale triggered the appearance of a "Submit Response" button.

After submitting their response, participants were shown the actual outcome: a segmented color band indicating either a strong decrease in inflammation (-10), no change (0), or a strong increase (+10) in inflammation, displayed for two seconds.
Additionally, a text appeared above the outcome stating: "The outcome of this meal on inflammation is:".
After completing a training stage, participants proceeded to a test stage, which was introduced by the following instructions:
For the next part of the experiment, you should continue to make predictions about the effect a meal has on inflammation.
However, in this part, you will NOT receive any feedback.
You will also be asked to indicate how confident you are in your predictions, from not confident at all (0) to very confident (10).
Press the space bar to continue the experiment.
Each cue was presented once for the expectation test and again in the subsequent trial for the confidence test.
Expectation test trials were identical to the training trials, except that no outcome was presented following the submission of the expectation.

Instead, after submitting their expectation, participants were shown the rated cue and their selected rating: "You just rated that you expect the outcome of this meal on inflammation to be:" (with the expectation rating's value displayed on the next line).
They were then asked to rate their confidence about this prediction: "How confident are you in your rating?"
Confidence was rated on an 11point scale ranging from "0: not confident at all" to "10: very confident."
In all rating scales used throughout the experiment, only the midpoint and the extreme ends displayed numerical labels.
At the end of the experiment, participants' understanding of the task and whether they had used notes during the task were assessed.
Understanding was tested at the end to avoid any potential influence on learning.

Experiment 2 had two aims.
The first was to replicate the compound test results from Experiment 1.
The second was to assess confidence before the compound training using a potentially more sensitive measure.
To this end, a forced-choice method was used, as in Spicer et al. (2022, Experiment 4).

text.text: In this forced-choice confidence test, participants were shown the outcome expectation ratings they had given for cues A and B and were required to choose whether they felt more confident in their rating for A or in their rating for B.

If the Training 1 schedules for cues A and B produced a difference in relative certainty that was not fully captured by the confidence measure used in Experiment 1, such a difference should be more likely to be detected with a forced-choice measure.
Apart from this change at Test 1, Experiment 2 was identical to Experiment 1.
The predictions were thus identical to those in Experiment 1.

An a priori power analysis for the primary comparison between AD and BC indicated a target sample size of 80 participants.
This sample size provided 87% power to detect the effect observed in Experiment 1 (Cohen's dz = 0.35), at α = .05.

A sensitivity analysis for the planned two-tailed exact binomial test of the forced-choice responses further indicated that, with N = 80, α = .05, and 87% power, the study could detect a medium effect, Cohen's g = .177.
This corresponds to a true choice proportion of approximately .677 relative to the chance-level proportion of p0 = .50.

text.text: Experiment 3 was therefore designed to increase certainty about the causal status of A and, consequently, to increase the relative-certainty difference between A and B before the compound training.
Specifically, Experiment 3 replaced the EW0 trials used in Experiments 1 and 2 with W-10 trials, while retaining the AW+10 trials.

Presenting W both alone and in compound with A was expected to make it easier for participants to attribute the strong increase in inflammation on AW+10 trials to A, thereby clarifying A's causal role.
Apart from this change, which was also applied to the corresponding control cue C, the training schedule in Experiment 3 was identical to that used in Experiments 1 and 2.

If the absence of theory protection in Experiments 1 and 2 reflected an insufficient difference in relative certainty between A and B, then increasing certainty about A should increase the likelihood of observing theory protection.

Therefore, if training A with AW+10 and W-10 trials in Experiment 3 make participants more certain about A's causal status and thereby increase the difference in relative certainty between A and B, then, according to the theory protection account (e.g., Spicer et al., 2020 Spicer et al., , 2022)), this should lead to lower outcome expectation ratings for BC than for AD at the final test.

Thus far, we have interpreted the present findings primarily within an associative-learning framework, according to which repeated cue-outcome pairings lead to the formation and modification of associations, with learning determined by prediction error (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972; Rescorla, 2000 Rescorla, , 2001)).

text.text: An alternative perspective is provided by propositional and causal-model accounts of human associative learning, which emphasize that learners may reason about relations between events and use assumptions about causal structure when interpreting new evidence (e.g., Booth & Buehner, 2007; Griffiths & Tenenbaum, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Waldmann & Holyoak, 1992).

text.text: From this perspective, participants may have used the relatively transparent causal structure of the present tasks and the limited number of cues to infer specific relations between individual foods and outcomes and to derive their test ratings accordingly.
Considered within this framework, confidence may be better understood as part of a broader reasoning process rather than as a separate mechanism that directly determines learning.
Confidence may signal how well specified participants' hypotheses are about a cue's causal role, given the instructions, task structure, training histories, and plausible cue-outcome relations.
However, how participants attribute new evidence may not depend on confidence alone.
Instead, it may depend on whether the task structure provides a plausible way to assign the unexpected outcome to one cue rather than another.
Future experiments could directly assess participants' causal hypotheses and test this possibility more directly.

In conclusion, the present findings were more consistent with an individual prediction error account (e.g., Rescorla, 2000 Rescorla, , 2001) ) than with the theory protection account (e.g., Spicer et al., 2020 Spicer et al., , 2022)).

text.text: Across Experiments 1, 2, 5, and 6, the cue generating the larger individual prediction error generally showed greater associative change, even when participants were relatively more certain about that cue.

Experiment 3 provided the clearest evidence for a pattern consistent with theory protection, but Experiment 4 failed to replicate this pattern despite showing the predicted difference in relative certainty between A and B. Thus, relative certainty did not consistently determine how learning was distributed across cues, challenging the generality of the role assigned to relative certainty in the theory protection account (e.g., Spicer et al., 2020 Spicer et al., , 2022)).

text.text: At the same time, these findings do not rule out a role for certainty in learning.
Rather, they suggest that the influence of certainty may depend on boundary conditions that remain to be specified.

One possibility is that theory protection requires not relative certainty alone, but a particular configuration of absolute certainty, in which one cue is held with sufficiently high confidence and another remains sufficiently uncertain.
Future research should therefore identify when learning is primarily determined by individual prediction error and under what conditions certainty shapes the distribution of learning across cues.

text.text: This possibility may help explain the change in the AD-BC pattern across Experiments 1-4.

Across these experiments, the critical procedural change concerned the training of cue A. In Experiments 3 and 4, A was trained with AW+10 and W-10 trials, whereas in Experiments 1 and 2, A was trained with AW+10 and EW0 trials.The former schedule may have supported a more pronounced association between A and a strong increase in inflammation and, consequently, a larger individual prediction error when AB-10 trials were later presented.

If this prediction error exceeded the threshold required to trigger a rapid attentional shift, attention may have shifted away from A, limiting further learning about A and allowing greater learning to accrue to B.
